subject.title: Defensive security practice on systems you own
subject.framing: This subject teaches people how to understand, reduce, and observe risk on devices, accounts, and networks they control or are explicitly authorized to protect. It is oriented toward consent-based practice: inventory, boundaries, least privilege, recovery readiness, and safe observation. It is not an offense cookbook. The existing Showmob page defensive-local-security-lab already proved the topic is teachable as practice, but it compressed consent, topology, listener inventory, sensors, and honeypot gates into a single page. Research here surfaces why that compression was forced: the subject has many natural seams (identity, device surface, network zones, observation, decoys, cloud accounts, travel/shared networks, incident recovery) that a blind scope pass should be able to find without being told a page count.

whoArrives: Curious home users who want a clearer picture of their own network and accounts
Hobbyists with a spare Pi, travel router, or old laptop who want a reversible lab
Small-team operators (family IT, indie shop, volunteer org) without a security team
Developers who ship software and need defensive instincts for the systems they run
Privacy-conscious individuals who care more about exposure and retention than red-team glory
likelyAlreadyKnow: Basic OS use (install apps, change Wi-Fi, find settings)
That passwords and updates matter, even if practice is inconsistent
Rough idea that home routers, phones, and cloud accounts are connected
How to open a terminal or Settings and follow a short checklist
likelyDoNotKnow: Difference between a listening service, an open port, and an exposed path
Why network zones and outbound deny matter before any decoy
How consent and authorization bound what monitoring is legal and ethical
What 'recovery ready' means beyond having a password manager
How standards frameworks (CSF, CIS, OWASP) map to home-scale practice
audienceAssumptions.readingStance: Willing to do things on owned gear; not looking for unauthorized access methods; may be intimidated by jargon and by fear of breaking their network.

deliberatelyExcluded.why: Consent is the first control; shared networks require a boundary the learner controls.

deliberatelyExcluded.item: Offense-oriented CTF playbooks framed as 'how to break in'
deliberatelyExcluded.why: Wrong job for this series; would invert the teaching goal.

deliberatelyExcluded.item: Malware authorship, keyloggers, stealth persistence how-tos
deliberatelyExcluded.why: Dual-use and surveillance-theft adjacent; out of scope even as fiction.

perspectives.name: Home lab defender
caresAbout: Seeing listeners and zones without breaking family Wi-Fi
Clear consent rules when roommates share upstream internet
misses: Cloud account takeover paths that never touch the home lab
Organizational policy and evidence retention expectations

perspectives.name: Small-team operator
caresAbout: Cheap controls that survive busy weeks
misses: Deep packet craft and sensor tuning
Formal compliance mapping unless a contract forces it
Personal privacy tradeoffs that differ from business risk

perspectives.name: Privacy-conscious individual
caresAbout: Who can see location, messages, and backups
Avoiding tools that become surveillance of themselves or household members
misses: Detection value of limited, consented logs
Recovery after lockout when privacy hardening removes fallback paths
That isolation and observability are complementary, not opposites

perspectives.name: Incident responder (home / small scale)
caresAbout: What changed, when, and what to preserve
Containment without destroying evidence they need for recovery
Knowing who to call (bank, cloud provider, device maker) and in what order
misses: Prevention basics that would have shrunk the blast radius
Steady-state hygiene that never feels like an 'incident'

perspectives.name: Standards / compliance-aware reader
caresAbout: Mapping practice to named outcomes (identify, protect, detect, respond, recover)
Checklists that auditors or insurers recognize at a high level
misses: That home labs need reversible experiments more than binder-ready policy
Overfitting enterprise controls onto a single household

perspectives.name: Developer who also operates what they ship
caresAbout: Exposed admin panels and default credentials on side projects
Same mental model for laptop, VPS, and home server
misses: Physical and household shared-network consent issues
Family-device and IoT inventory as first-class risk

concepts.name: Consent and authorization boundary
concepts.briefMeaning: You only observe, configure, or experiment on equipment and traffic you own or are explicitly authorized to touch. On shared networks, put the lab behind a router you control.

concepts.name: Asset and identity inventory
concepts.briefMeaning: A dated list of devices, accounts, admins, and 'what this is for' — the baseline everything else compares against.

concepts.name: Listening-service inventory
concepts.briefMeaning: On owned hosts, list processes bound to network sockets; distinguish loopback-only from LAN- or WAN-reachable; document why each exists.

concepts.name: Attack surface (defensive view)
concepts.briefMeaning: The set of ways an unauthorized party could interact with your systems: exposed services, weak identities, physical access, supply-chain defaults, recovery paths.

concepts.name: Network zones and segmentation
concepts.briefMeaning: Separate trust levels (trusted devices, guest, IoT, lab/decoy) with routing and firewall rules you can verify from both sides — not just a 'guest SSID' label.

concepts.name: Topology verification
concepts.briefMeaning: Prove the boundary works: lab cannot reach protected LANs; decoy cannot phone home; admin paths are intentional.

concepts.name: Identity and authentication
concepts.briefMeaning: Who can act as you: passwords, passkeys, MFA, session cookies, device trust, recovery codes — and how takeover usually happens through recovery or reuse.

concepts.name: Account hygiene
concepts.briefMeaning: Unique credentials, MFA where available, remove unused admins and OAuth grants, prefer passkeys or app-based MFA over SMS when practical.

concepts.name: Session and device trust lifecycle
concepts.briefMeaning: Signed-in sessions, remembered devices, and API tokens outlive password changes unless you revoke them; inventory and kill stale trust.

concepts.name: Least privilege and role separation
concepts.briefMeaning: Daily work uses non-admin accounts; services run with minimal rights; shared 'family admin' passwords are a single point of failure.

concepts.name: Patch, firmware, and default credentials
concepts.briefMeaning: Routers, cameras, NAS, and IoT often ship with known defaults and rare updates; update cadence and credential change are first-line protect controls.

concepts.name: Secrets handling
concepts.briefMeaning: Passwords, API keys, backup codes, and SSH keys must not live in chat, screenshots, or public repos; rotate when exposed.

concepts.name: Backup, integrity, and restore practice
concepts.briefMeaning: Backups that have never been restored are theory; ransomware and lockout make restore drills a protect-and-recover control.

concepts.name: Passive observation and metadata-first sensing
concepts.briefMeaning: On authorized segments, collect connection and protocol metadata before deep content capture; limit retention; know what the sensor cannot see (encrypted payloads).

concepts.name: Sensor and decoy choice
concepts.briefMeaning: Pick the smallest useful tool: rich connection logs vs alert-oriented IDS vs lightweight decoy services — match job to tool, one at a time.

concepts.name: Baselines and anomaly readiness
concepts.briefMeaning: Without a dated 'normal', every alert is noise; baselines cover listeners, zones, and typical outbound destinations for owned devices.

concepts.name: Change as evidence
concepts.briefMeaning: Security practice is comparative: what differed after an update, a new device, or a suspected compromise.

concepts.name: Decoy / honeypot containment
concepts.briefMeaning: A decoy is only educational if isolated, outbound-denied, free of real secrets, LAN-first, and paired with defined retention and review.

concepts.name: Outbound deny by default for untrusted roles
concepts.briefMeaning: Untrusted or decoy systems must not become launch points; verify egress blocks, not just inbound filters.

concepts.name: Observation ethics and retention
concepts.briefMeaning: Logs can become household surveillance; define purpose, who can read, how long kept, and when deleted — especially on shared family networks.

concepts.name: Privacy vs detection tension
concepts.briefMeaning: More visibility can improve detection and also increase sensitive retention; resolve with consent, minimization, and zone design — not by ignoring either side.

concepts.name: Shared and untrusted upstream networks
concepts.briefMeaning: Roommates, cafes, hotels, and family Wi-Fi change what you can safely observe and what you must assume about the path to the internet.

concepts.name: Travel laptop / phone hardening
concepts.briefMeaning: Assume hostile or curious networks; prefer full-disk encryption, screen lock, VPN only where trusted, and avoid admin tasks on untrusted Wi-Fi.

concepts.name: IoT and always-on edge devices
concepts.briefMeaning: Cameras, speakers, printers, and smart plugs expand surface with weak update stories; zone them away from trusted workstations when possible.

concepts.name: Cloud account takeover recovery
concepts.briefMeaning: Recovery order matters: regain auth, revoke sessions and apps, rotate secrets, check forwarding rules and MFA changes, then restore from known-good state.

concepts.name: Containment without self-sabotage
concepts.briefMeaning: Isolate first when compromise is plausible; avoid panic reimaging that destroys the only evidence of what was taken; document actions.

concepts.name: Recovery readiness
concepts.briefMeaning: Printed or offline recovery codes, secondary admin, tested backups, and known contacts — established before the incident, not during it.

concepts.name: Developer-operator surface
concepts.briefMeaning: Side projects, home servers, CI tokens, and exposed admin UIs are often the learner's largest real surface — same controls as 'security lab', applied to what they already run.

concepts.name: Standards mapped to home scale
concepts.briefMeaning: NIST CSF functions and CIS-style hygiene translate to household verbs (inventory, protect, detect, respond, recover) without requiring enterprise tooling.

concepts.name: Ransomware and destructive pattern (defensive)
concepts.briefMeaning: Understand the pattern as backup integrity + privilege + remote access failure — teach prevention and restore drills, not payload analysis.

concepts.name: Remote access paths
concepts.briefMeaning: VPN, reverse proxies, cloud tunnels, RDP/SSH, and vendor 'remote support' are intentional doors; inventory them like listeners.

concepts.name: Physical access and lost-device reality
concepts.briefMeaning: Theft and shoulder-surfing defeat purely network-centric advice; encryption at rest and remote wipe plans matter.

concepts.name: Supply-chain and vendor defaults
concepts.briefMeaning: Preinstalled apps, OEM remote management, and 'smart' features create surface the owner never chose; inventory and disable what you do not need.

concepts.name: Tool theater vs verified controls
concepts.briefMeaning: Installing a sensor or VPN without verifying zones, listeners, and recovery readiness creates a false sense of safety.

dependencies.why: Zones only make ethical sense once the authorized observation set is defined.
Sensors without consent turn into unauthorized interception.
Decoys sit inside the same authorization story as the lab.
You need a device list before socket inventories are meaningful.
Baselines are differences against a dated inventory.
Exposed listeners are a primary surface component on owned hosts.
Unverified segmentation is theater.
Egress policy is part of zone design for untrusted roles.
Containment claims require proof from both sides.
A decoy that can phone home is a liability.
Hygiene is the daily practice of identity controls.
Sessions and device trust extend identity beyond passwords.
Recovery assumes you know how accounts were secured and what to revoke.
Revoking stale sessions is a recovery step, not optional cleanup.
Destructive malware amplifies when every process runs as admin.
Restore drills are how backups become recovery.
Integrity-checked offline or versioned backups are the main recover control.
Logs without a notion of normal cannot detect meaningful change.
Tool choice follows the observation job.
Decoy tools are a sensor class with stricter containment needs.
Containment decisions need a before/after picture.
Retention and purpose limits are how the tension is managed.
Travel is the extreme case of untrusted upstream.
Shared upstream forces a personal boundary device.
IoT is the common reason households need more than one trust zone.
IoT risk is dominated by update and default-credential failure.
Intentional doors are still surface.
Leaked tokens are a top developer-operator failure mode.
Offline codes and secondary admins must exist before lockout.
Containment without a recovery plan stalls at isolation.
Verification is the antidote to tool theater.
CSF Identify maps cleanly to inventory at home scale.
Lost/stolen devices are a travel-class risk year-round.
You cannot disable what you have not listed.

examples.situation: Inventory listeners on a personal Linux/macOS/Windows machine after installing a game launcher and a remote-access helper.
Place a Pi sensor and a spare laptop behind a travel router on a roommate-shared upstream, verify isolation both ways.
examples.consentNote: Only lab segment observed; roommate traffic stays upstream of the lab router.

examples.situation: Move cameras and smart plugs to a guest/IoT SSID with no access to work laptops; confirm printer still works for intended devices only.
examples.consentNote: Household-owned devices; discuss with household before changing shared Wi-Fi.

examples.situation: Work from a hotel network: full-disk encryption on, avoid admin banking over captive portal, use personal hotspot when doing sensitive mail.
examples.consentNote: Learner's own devices; no monitoring of hotel patrons.

examples.situation: Suspicious forwarding rule appears in personal email; regain access, revoke sessions, kill unknown OAuth apps, rotate password and MFA, check sent mail.
New home NAS still on vendor default admin; change creds, disable WAN management, put on trusted zone, inventory shares.
Hobby VPS still has an admin panel on a public IP with a weak password from a tutorial; lock down SSH keys, remove panel exposure, rotate secrets that were in the repo once.
examples.consentNote: VPS and repo owned by the learner.

examples.situation: Quarterly restore of one important folder from backup to a scratch location; time it; note what failed.
After zones and listeners are documented, add one LAN-only decoy with outbound denied; review its alerts for a week; delete logs on schedule.
examples.consentNote: Only inside learner-controlled lab; no internet exposure.

examples.situation: Phone missing after a trip; use find/wipe, revoke app sessions from another device, check authenticator backup plan.

analogies.analogy: Network zones are rooms with doors; a guest SSID without firewall rules is a hallway labeled 'guest' with no door. Outbound deny for a decoy is boarding up the window so a stranger who entered the mudroom cannot leave with your keys.
You cannot tell if a wrench is missing until you had a tool inventory. Listener and asset inventories are the same idea for digital doors.
Monitoring without a consent boundary is like pointing cameras into a neighbor's yard because their Wi-Fi is nearby. The travel router is your fence.

A passive sensor is a smoke detector; a honeypot is a labeled drill prop in a locked room. Neither replaces extinguishers (backups, MFA, patching), and wiring a drill prop to the gas main is how labs go wrong.
Recovery codes are spare keys stored somewhere other than under the mat. MFA without offline recovery is a lock that locks you out when the phone dies.

Full packet capture on family Wi-Fi can be as intimate as reading someone's mail 'for safety.' Metadata-first, purpose-limited, zone-scoped observation is the difference between a smoke alarm and opening their letters.
Tool theater installs impressive gear in view of the audience; verified controls are stage crew checks nobody applauds — proving the trap door is bolted before the decoy scene.

misconceptions.belief: A guest Wi-Fi name means devices are isolated.
misconceptions.whyItFails: Many consumer routers still allow guest-to-LAN or device-to-device paths; labels are not firewall proofs.

misconceptions.belief: A VPN makes the device and home network 'secure.'
misconceptions.whyItFails: A VPN mainly changes path trust to a provider; it does not patch listeners, fix defaults, or restore backups.

misconceptions.belief: Antivirus alone covers modern account and cloud risk.
misconceptions.whyItFails: Most consumer takeovers are credential, session, or recovery-path failures, not local malware signatures.

misconceptions.belief: The exciting first step is deploying a honeypot.
misconceptions.whyItFails: Without zones, outbound deny, and baselines, a decoy can become a launch point or a retention mess.

misconceptions.belief: Anything bound to localhost cannot matter.
misconceptions.whyItFails: Local services still expand risk with malicious local code, misbound interfaces, and container port publishes that escape intent.

misconceptions.belief: MFA means the account cannot be taken over.
misconceptions.whyItFails: Prompt bombing, SIM swap on SMS MFA, session theft, and recovery-flow weaknesses still succeed; MFA reduces risk, it does not erase it.

misconceptions.belief: Keep everything forever; more logs always equal more security.
misconceptions.whyItFails: Unbounded retention increases privacy harm and search noise; purpose and deletion schedules are part of the control.

misconceptions.belief: Cheap IoT is too simple to be a real risk.
misconceptions.whyItFails: Always-on, rarely updated devices with defaults become durable footholds and lateral paths on flat networks.

misconceptions.belief: You must learn offense to practice defense.
misconceptions.whyItFails: Most home and small-team wins are inventory, identity, zones, backups, and recovery — none require exploit craft.

misconceptions.belief: Changing the password automatically signs out every other device and app.
misconceptions.whyItFails: Many services keep sessions and OAuth grants until explicitly revoked.

misconceptions.belief: Having a backup product enabled means you can recover.
misconceptions.whyItFails: Untested restores fail on credentials, incomplete selections, or ransomware-reachable sync folders.

misconceptions.belief: One shared family admin password is fine because it is 'just home.'
misconceptions.whyItFails: It couples every person's risk and makes offboarding (breakups, roommates leaving, kid devices) painful and unsafe.

edgeCases.boundary: ISP CGNAT, mesh Wi-Fi, or ISP-managed routers hide or restrict true boundary control.
edgeCases.breaksNaiveAdvice: Advice that assumes you can set VLANs or mirror ports on the only router may be impossible without adding your own downstream router.

edgeCases.boundary: Household includes employer-managed laptops or partner-owned phones.
edgeCases.breaksNaiveAdvice: 'Inventory everything on the Wi-Fi' can violate policy or consent; teach device ownership tags and lab isolation instead.

edgeCases.boundary: Authenticator lives only on the phone that was just lost.
edgeCases.breaksNaiveAdvice: Hardening without offline recovery codes creates lockout; recovery readiness must be taught with MFA, not after.

edgeCases.boundary: DoH/DoT and always-on VPN change what a home sensor can see.
edgeCases.breaksNaiveAdvice: Expecting full DNS visibility from a LAN sensor fails; teach what metadata remains and what does not.

edgeCases.boundary: Homelab enthusiast already has VLANs but no documentation.
edgeCases.breaksNaiveAdvice: Complex undocumented zones are harder to verify than a simple travel-router lab; documentation becomes the foundation.

edgeCases.boundary: Household includes minors; monitoring intersects safety and privacy laws/norms.
edgeCases.breaksNaiveAdvice: Blanket packet capture advice is inappropriate; prefer device controls, zones, and transparent household agreements.

edgeCases.boundary: No self-hosted gear; everything is phones + cloud accounts.
edgeCases.breaksNaiveAdvice: Pi/honeypot tutorials miss the real surface; identity, sessions, and recovery dominate.

edgeCases.boundary: Couples or teams share a vault incorrectly (one login for all).
edgeCases.breaksNaiveAdvice: Password manager adoption without individual accounts and emergency access design recreates single-point failure.

realWorldFailures.pattern: Credential stuffing against reused passwords on consumer and small-business sites
realWorldFailures.whatBroke: Password reuse + slow breach response; accounts taken without malware on the device

realWorldFailures.pattern: SIM swap and SMS-based account recovery abuse
realWorldFailures.whatBroke: Phone number treated as a strong identity; recovery flow weaker than primary MFA

realWorldFailures.pattern: Internet-exposed remote desktop / admin panels with weak or default credentials
realWorldFailures.whatBroke: Remote access path left open; ransomware and botnets followed

realWorldFailures.pattern: IoT botnets built from default credentials and unpatched firmwares (Mirai-class pattern)
realWorldFailures.whatBroke: Always-on devices with defaults on flat networks; owners unaware they were enrolled

realWorldFailures.pattern: Consumer router compromise via outdated firmware or remote management left on
realWorldFailures.whatBroke: Single chokepoint device; DNS or traffic redirected; all household devices affected

realWorldFailures.pattern: Malicious or overly broad OAuth app grants and forgotten third-party access
realWorldFailures.whatBroke: Password stayed secret while mail/drive access persisted via tokens

realWorldFailures.pattern: Ransomware encrypts live sync folders and online-only backups reachable with the same credentials
realWorldFailures.whatBroke: Backup design lacked offline/versioned/immutable copy; restore failed when needed

realWorldFailures.pattern: Public cloud storage or admin interfaces left open by misconfiguration (small teams and solo devs)
realWorldFailures.whatBroke: Default-open mental model; no listener/remote-access inventory for cloud resources

realWorldFailures.pattern: Shared credentials and unmanaged ex-household or ex-coworker access
realWorldFailures.whatBroke: No offboarding; 'trust' substituted for accounts and zones

practiceOpenings.moment: Before buying gear: draw the real network, mark ownership and consent, list devices.
On one owned computer, run a listener inventory, save a dated baseline, explain each unknown before changing anything.
Change default router admin password, disable remote WAN admin if present, note firmware version and update path.
Move the top five accounts into a password manager; turn on non-SMS MFA where offered; store recovery codes offline.
On one cloud account, review active sessions and third-party apps; revoke anything unrecognized.
If the router supports it, move one camera or plug to guest/IoT and verify it cannot reach a work laptop.
Put a spare device behind a travel router; verify upstream roommate network is not being inspected.
Restore one folder from backup to a scratch path; write down time-to-recover and gaps.
After zones exist, add one passive metadata sensor on the lab segment only; review retention settings day one.
Only after verification: deploy one contained decoy, walk the honeypot safety gates checklist, keep outbound denied.

visualCandidates.what: Annotated home topology: upstream ISP, household LAN, lab router, trusted / IoT / decoy zones, with ownership and consent labels on each link.
visualCandidates.whyPicture: Consent and zones are spatial; prose lists hide the boundary.
visualCandidates.missingPrimitiveNote: Showmob diagram is a linear node list; needs annotated figure / floor-map style (already flagged as earned primitive in LEARNING-ARCHITECTURE.md). Existing lab page used image+SVG for this reason.

visualCandidates.what: Branching cause chain: phishing or reuse → session/token → forwarding rule → lockout, with defensive cut-points marked.
visualCandidates.whyPicture: Account takeover is multi-step; readers need to see where revoke/MFA/recovery codes cut the chain.
visualCandidates.missingPrimitiveNote: Branching cause chain is explicitly called out as beyond linear diagram nodes.

visualCandidates.what: Before/after compact table of listeners with process, bind address, reachability, justified?
visualCandidates.whyPicture: Comparison over time; table/comparison blocks may suffice.

visualCandidates.what: Safety gates as a sequential gate diagram (isolation → outbound deny → no secrets → LAN-only → retention).
visualCandidates.whyPicture: Order matters; checklist alone understates sequence dependence.
visualCandidates.missingPrimitiveNote: Checklist or steps may be enough; annotated figure nicer but not required.

visualCandidates.what: NIST CSF five functions mapped to household verbs and example practices.
visualCandidates.whyPicture: Standards feel abstract until drawn as a cycle with home examples.

visualCandidates.what: Visual tension between retention depth and privacy harm, with minimization sweet spot.
visualCandidates.whyPicture: Tradeoff is easier as a continuum than as a moral lecture.
visualCandidates.missingPrimitiveNote: No continuum/annotated-axis primitive; comparison or custom image workaround.

naturalBoundaries.seam: Consent, authorization, and what 'defensive' means — the gate before any tool.
naturalBoundaries.whyNatural: Without this seam, every later practice can drift into unauthorized monitoring.

naturalBoundaries.seam: Asset, identity, and listener inventory — establish baselines.
naturalBoundaries.whyNatural: The existing lab page already starts here; it is a complete teaching job before zones get deep.

naturalBoundaries.seam: Authentication, MFA, sessions, secrets, and cloud account recovery.
naturalBoundaries.whyNatural: Cloud-only households never need a Pi lab; this seam is a whole course track on its own.

naturalBoundaries.seam: Segmentation, topology proof, IoT placement, shared-upstream boundaries.
naturalBoundaries.whyNatural: Distinct skills from identity; matches the lab page's topology half without the decoy.

naturalBoundaries.seam: Passive sensing, baselines, retention ethics, privacy vs detection.
naturalBoundaries.whyNatural: Sensors are a different mode (how-to + ethics) from building zones.

naturalBoundaries.seam: Honeypot/decoy practice only after gates; outbound deny; LAN-first.
naturalBoundaries.whyNatural: The existing page crammed this with everything else; it is an advanced, optional seam that depends on prior verification.

naturalBoundaries.seam: Travel networks, lost devices, physical access assumptions.
naturalBoundaries.whyNatural: Different environment and threat assumptions than a static home lab.

naturalBoundaries.seam: Backups, ransomware-pattern defense, incident containment, recovery readiness.
naturalBoundaries.whyNatural: Respond/recover are CSF-distinct from protect/detect; practice openings differ.

naturalBoundaries.seam: Side projects, VPS, CI secrets, exposed admin UIs — same defensive verbs, different surface.
naturalBoundaries.whyNatural: Audience fork: many Showmob readers are builders; this seam keeps them without forcing honeypots.

naturalBoundaries.seam: Map household practice to CSF / CIS / OWASP high-level language for readers who need vocabulary for work or insurance.
naturalBoundaries.whyNatural: Optional advanced bridge; not required to practice, but a clear explanatory seam.

compressionNote.whyCourseShaped: Each bundled piece has different prerequisites, practice openings, failure modes, and visuals. Consent and inventory do not require a decoy. Identity/cloud recovery barely appears yet dominates real household incidents. Scope should be able to discover multiple seams from research density alone — that is the Phase 2 blind test.
